props.title: House
props.initialSlug: Haunted house turns grief into surreal nightmare

sections.content: House (1985) stands as one of Japanese cinema's most gleefully unhinged haunted house films. Director Nobuhiko Obayashi unleashed a psychedelic nightmare filled with killer pianos, dancing skeletons, and a man-eating house - using deliberately artificial effects that feel like a fever dream. This experimental approach influenced later genre-bending horror like Evil Dead II (1987) and Hausu directly inspired the surreal horror elements in Beetlejuice (1988). The film's candy-colored palette and dreamlike logic created a new template for Asian horror that would later influence films like Uzumaki (2000) and Tag (2015).

sections.content: The 1980s Japanese experimental film scene gave birth to several boundary-pushing horror works, but none matched House's fearless combination of pop art aesthetics and horror elements. Director Obayashi incorporated his background in TV commercials, using rapid cuts, animation, and deliberately artificial effects. This approach influenced later Japanese experimentalists like Shinya Tsukamoto's Tetsuo: The Iron Man (1989) and Sogo Ishii's Electric Dragon 80.000 V (2001).

The film's influence extends beyond Japan, particularly in its use of practical effects and surreal imagery. Peter Jackson's early splatter films like Bad Taste (1987) and Meet the Feebles (1989) share similar DNA in their gleeful mixture of horror and absurdist comedy. Modern filmmakers like Panos Cosmatos (Mandy (2018)) and Justin Benson/Aaron Moorhead (Spring (2014)) continue drawing inspiration from House's fearless experimentation. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Japanese Experimental Horror

sections.content: House helped establish a distinctly Japanese approach to horror that prioritized atmosphere and surrealism over conventional scares. This influence can be traced through works like Kiyoshi Kurosawa's Cure (1997) and Takashi Miike's Gozu (2003), where reality becomes increasingly unstable. The film's impact on modern J-horror extends to Sion Sono's Strange Circus (2005) and Tag (2015), which embrace similar techniques of reality-bending horror.
